theme: The crucifixion; the burial, the King dies for his people
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 27:32-66. Jesus is crucified, mocked, abandoned, and dies. The temple curtain is torn, the earth shakes, and a centurion confesses. Read this slowly and quietly. Then notice the burial and the guard at the tomb.
settingTheScene: Jesus is led to Golgotha, “the place of a skull,” and crucified between two robbers. Matthew tells the story with restraint, but with signs that show its cosmic meaning. Darkness covers the land, the temple veil splits, the earth quakes, and the dead are raised. The King dies for his people.
observation: “And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, This is Jesus, the King of the Jews” (27:37).
“He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him” (27:42).
“Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour” (27:45).
“Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani? That is, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (27:46).
“And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit” (27:50).
“And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (27:51).
“Truly this was the Son of God!” (27:54).
“Make it as secure as you can” (27:65).
interpretation:
The mocking is cruel and ironic. The leaders say, “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” They are right in a way they do not realize. He did not save himself precisely because he was saving others. The sign over his head, “King of the Jews,” is written as a mockery and is true.

At noon, darkness falls over the land for three hours. At the ninth hour, Jesus cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” This is the opening of Psalm 22. It is the cry of one bearing the weight of sin. The Son who has never been separated from the Father experiences the abandonment that we deserve. This is the heart of the atonement. He bore the wrath for his people.

Then he yields up his spirit. Matthew records what follows. The temple curtain, which separated the Holy of Holies from the people, is torn from top to bottom, by God. The way into God’s presence is open. The earth shakes, the rocks split, and tombs open: the power of death is broken. A Roman centurion who watched him die says, “Truly this was the Son of God!” The first confession after the cross is from a Gentile.

Women who followed Jesus watch from a distance. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in clean linen, and lays it in his own new tomb. The chief priests, who remembered that Jesus said he would rise on the third day, ask Pilate for a guard and seal the stone. They do all they can to keep him in the grave. But human security cannot stop God’s plan.

The chapter ends in silence. It is Saturday. The King is dead and buried. The disciples are scattered. And the reader holds their breath.
connection: Psalm 22 describes the crucifixion in detail, from the cry of abandonment to the mocking and the casting of lots. Isaiah 53:4-6 and 10-12 describe the servant bearing our sins. Hebrews 10:19-22 says that through the curtain, that is, his flesh, we have confidence to enter the holy places. Galatians 3:13 says Christ became a curse for us. Romans 5:8. 1 Peter 3:18. 2 Corinthians 5:21. Mark 15:39 gives the centurion’s confession.
application:
Spend a few minutes in silence with this chapter. Let the weight of it settle.

Say aloud, “He did this for me,” and thank him specifically.

Because the curtain is torn, come boldly into God’s presence in prayer today.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being forsaken so that you never would be.
Tell him what it means that he bore your sin and the wrath you deserved.
Sit in silence for a moment, and let it settle.
